l: The First Book of Samuel, The First Book of Samuel, Chapter 10
s: Samuel anoints Saul with oil, declares him prince over the LORD's inheritance, and gives him a series of signs: men at Rachel's tomb, three men at the oak of Tabor, and a band of prophets near the hill of God. All the signs come true that day, Saul is given another heart and prophesies among the prophets, which gives rise to the proverb "Is Saul also among the prophets?" Saul tells his uncle only about the donkeys and not about the kingdom. At Mizpah Samuel rebukes Israel for rejecting God by asking for a king, and lots are cast until Saul, hiding among the baggage, is chosen. The people shout "Long live the king!", Samuel records the regulations of the kingdom, and Saul goes home to Gibeah, where some worthless fellows despise him but he holds his peace.

l: Samuel, The First Book of Samuel, Chapter 10
s: Samuel pours oil on Saul's head, kisses him, and gives him signs and instructions, including to go down ahead of him to Gilgal and wait seven days. He gathers the people at Mizpah, rebukes them for rejecting God, presents Saul as the LORD's chosen, and writes the regulations of the kingdom in a book laid up before the LORD.

l: Saul, The First Book of Samuel, Chapter 10
s: Saul is anointed, experiences all the promised signs, receives another heart, and prophesies among the prophets, prompting the proverb "Is Saul also among the prophets?" He keeps the kingdom matter secret from his uncle, hides among the baggage when chosen by lot at Mizpah, and stands head and shoulders above the people. He is acclaimed king, returns to Gibeah, and holds his peace when worthless fellows despise him.

l: LORD, The First Book of Samuel, Chapter 10
s: The LORD is said to have anointed Saul as prince over his inheritance, and his Spirit comes mightily on Saul. Samuel relays that the LORD brought Israel out of Egypt and that the people rejected him by demanding a king. When asked, the LORD reveals that Saul is hidden among the baggage, and the lot process picks Saul as his chosen one.

l: Israel, The First Book of Samuel, Chapter 10
s: Israel is reminded that God delivered them from Egypt and all oppressing kingdoms, yet they rejected him by asking for a king. They present themselves by tribes and thousands, shout "Long live the king!" at Saul's selection, and return to their houses. Some worthless fellows among them despise Saul and bring no tribute.

l: band of prophets (near the hill of God), The First Book of Samuel, Chapter 10
s: A band of prophets comes down from the high place with a lute, tambourine, pipe, and harp, prophesying, as Samuel foretold. Saul meets them, the Spirit of God comes on him, and he prophesies among them.

l: kingdom of Israel, The First Book of Samuel, Chapter 10
s: The kingdom begins as the people demand a king and Saul is chosen by lot at Mizpah and acclaimed. Samuel tells the people the regulations of the kingdom and writes them in a book laid up before the LORD. Saul is accompanied by an army whose hearts God had touched, though some despise him and bring no tribute.

l: Saul’s anointing, The First Book of Samuel, Chapter 10
s: Samuel anoints Saul privately by pouring a vial of oil on his head and kissing him, saying the LORD has anointed him prince over his inheritance. Signs follow that day, confirming it, and God gives Saul another heart. Saul keeps the matter secret from his uncle until the public choice at Mizpah.

l: The First Book of Samuel, The First Book of Samuel, Chapter 11
s: Nahash the Ammonite encamps against Jabesh Gilead and offers the men of Jabesh a covenant only if all their right eyes are gouged out. The elders win seven days to send messengers through Israel, and when the messengers reach Gibeah of Saul the people weep. Saul, coming from the field behind his oxen, is filled with God's Spirit and anger, cuts a yoke of oxen into pieces, and sends them through Israel to summon the people after Saul and Samuel. Israel musters at Bezek, Saul divides the people into three companies and routs the Ammonites the next morning, and Saul forbids putting to death those who had doubted him. At Samuel's urging the people go to Gilgal and make Saul king before the LORD, offering peace offerings and rejoicing.

l: Nahash the Ammonite, The First Book of Samuel, Chapter 11
s: Nahash encamps against Jabesh Gilead and demands that all the right eyes of its men be gouged out as the condition for a covenant, intending to dishonor all Israel. His forces are struck by Saul's army and scattered.

l: Jabesh Gilead, The First Book of Samuel, Chapter 11
s: Jabesh Gilead is besieged by Nahash the Ammonite. Its elders obtain seven days to seek help, and the town is rescued by Saul and Israel the next day, as promised.

l: inhabitants of Jabesh Gilead, The First Book of Samuel, Chapter 11
s: The men of Jabesh offer to serve Nahash, then learn the terms include losing their right eyes, so the elders send messengers across Israel. When promised rescue by the next day, they are glad and tell Nahash they will come out to him, and they are then delivered.

l: Saul, The First Book of Samuel, Chapter 11
s: Saul, coming in from the field behind his oxen, hears of Jabesh's plight, is seized by God's Spirit and anger, and summons Israel by sending pieces of a yoke of oxen. He leads the people in three companies to defeat the Ammonites, refuses to let anyone be put to death that day because the LORD rescued Israel, and is made king at Gilgal.

l: Samuel, The First Book of Samuel, Chapter 11
s: Samuel is named alongside Saul in the summons to war. After the victory the people ask him to bring forward those who doubted Saul's reign, and he instead tells them to go to Gilgal to renew the kingdom there.

l: Israel, The First Book of Samuel, Chapter 11
s: Israel, whose people weep at the news from Jabesh, come out as one man under the dread of the LORD, numbering three hundred thousand plus thirty thousand men of Judah at Bezek. They win the victory and then make Saul king at Gilgal, rejoicing greatly.

l: Ammonites, The First Book of Samuel, Chapter 11
s: The Ammonites, under Nahash, are attacked by Saul's three companies in the morning watch and struck until the heat of the day. The survivors are scattered so that no two are left together.

l: rescue of Jabesh (battle against the Ammonites), The First Book of Samuel, Chapter 11
s: After Israel musters at Bezek, messengers promise Jabesh rescue by the time the sun is hot the next day. Saul puts the people in three companies, enters the middle of the Ammonite camp in the morning watch, and routs them until the heat of the day.

l: Saul's coronation at Gilgal, The First Book of Samuel, Chapter 11
s: At Samuel's call to renew the kingdom, all the people go to Gilgal and make Saul king before the LORD. They offer peace offerings, and Saul and all the men of Israel rejoice greatly.

l: The First Book of Samuel, The First Book of Samuel, Chapter 12
s: Samuel addresses all Israel after a king has been set over them, noting that he is old and gray-headed and inviting them to testify against him; the people affirm he has not defrauded, oppressed, or taken anything from anyone. He recounts the LORD's righteous acts, from sending Moses and Aaron out of Egypt, through the people's forgetting and being sold to enemies, to the deliverers Jerubbaal, Bedan, Jephthah, and Samuel. He charges that when Nahash king of the Ammonites came against them, the people demanded a king though the LORD was their king. Samuel calls on the LORD to send thunder and rain during wheat harvest, and the people, terrified, confess their sin and ask him to pray for them. Samuel tells them not to fear, to keep serving the LORD with all their heart, promising to keep praying and instructing them, but warning that persistent evil will consume both them and their king.

l: Samuel, The First Book of Samuel, Chapter 12
s: Samuel reminds Israel that a king now walks before them, declares he is old and gray-headed, and has the people affirm he has taken nothing and oppressed no one. He recounts the LORD's saving acts, calls for thunder and rain as a sign, and, after the people's confession, tells them not to fear and promises to keep praying for them and to instruct them in the good and right way.

l: Israel, The First Book of Samuel, Chapter 12
s: Israel testifies that Samuel has not defrauded or oppressed them or taken anything from anyone's hand. Samuel charges them with having asked for a king when the LORD was their king, and after the thunder and rain they fear the LORD and Samuel, confess adding this evil to their sins, and ask Samuel to pray that they not die. They are told to keep following the LORD and are warned they will be consumed if they keep doing evil.

l: LORD, The First Book of Samuel, Chapter 12
s: The LORD is called as witness to Samuel's integrity and is recounted as having sent Moses and Aaron to bring the fathers out of Egypt, having sold forgetful Israel into enemy hands, and having sent Jerubbaal, Bedan, Jephthah, and Samuel to deliver them. He sends thunder and rain at Samuel's call, and Samuel says he will not forsake his people for his great name's sake, because it pleased him to make them a people for himself.

l: Saul, The First Book of Samuel, Chapter 12
s: The king, whom Israel chose and asked for, is described by Samuel as one the LORD has set over them. If people and king fear and serve the LORD, they are followers of the LORD their God; if they keep doing evil, both the people and their king will be consumed.

l: request for a king, The First Book of Samuel, Chapter 12
s: Samuel says Israel demanded a king when Nahash king of the Ammonites came against them, though the LORD was their king. Samuel calls it great wickedness in the LORD's sight, and the people afterward confess it as an evil added to all their sins, yet Samuel says the LORD will not forsake them.

l: thunder and rain, The First Book of Samuel, Chapter 12
s: Samuel announces during wheat harvest that he will call on the LORD to send thunder and rain so the people will see their wickedness in asking for a king. The LORD sends them that day, and all the people greatly fear the LORD and Samuel.

l: The First Book of Samuel, The First Book of Samuel, Chapter 13
s: Saul, who reigned over Israel forty-two years, chose three thousand men, and Jonathan struck the Philistine garrison in Geba, provoking the Philistines to gather a huge force at Michmash. Israel's frightened people hid or scattered while Saul waited at Gilgal for Samuel for seven days. When Samuel did not arrive, Saul offered the burnt offering himself, and Samuel then arrived and told him he had acted foolishly, that his kingdom would not continue, and that the LORD had sought a man after his own heart. Saul was left with about six hundred men at Geba while Philistine raiders went out in three companies. The chapter closes by explaining that the Philistines had left Israel without blacksmiths, so only Saul and Jonathan had a sword or spear on the day of battle.

l: Saul, The First Book of Samuel, Chapter 13
s: Saul, who reigned forty-two years, chose three thousand men and blew the trumpet after Jonathan's attack on the Philistine garrison. At Gilgal he grew afraid as the people scattered, offered the burnt offering himself instead of waiting for Samuel, and was told his kingdom would not continue. He was left with about six hundred men, and he and Jonathan were the only ones with a sword or spear.

l: Jonathan, The First Book of Samuel, Chapter 13
s: Jonathan led one thousand men at Gibeah of Benjamin and struck the Philistine garrison in Geba. He later stayed in Geba with Saul and the people, and he and Saul alone had a sword or spear on the day of battle.

l: Samuel, The First Book of Samuel, Chapter 13
s: Samuel had set the seven-day time for Saul's waiting at Gilgal but did not arrive until Saul had finished the burnt offering. He told Saul he had acted foolishly and not kept the LORD's commandment, and that his kingdom would not continue. He then left Gilgal for Gibeah of Benjamin.

l: LORD, The First Book of Samuel, Chapter 13
s: The LORD is said to have been ready to establish Saul's kingdom over Israel forever had Saul kept his commandment. Because Saul did not, the LORD has sought for himself a man after his own heart and appointed him prince over his people.

l: Philistines, The First Book of Samuel, Chapter 13
s: The Philistines responded to the strike on their Geba garrison by assembling thirty thousand chariots, six thousand horsemen, and people numerous as the sand, and they encamped at Michmash. They sent raiders out in three companies, and their garrison went to the pass of Michmash. They also prevented Israel from having blacksmiths so the Hebrews could not make swords or spears.

l: Israel, The First Book of Samuel, Chapter 13
s: Israel was gathered after Saul to Gilgal, having heard it was considered an abomination to the Philistines. Facing the Philistine army, the people hid in caves, thickets, rocks, tombs, and pits, some crossed the Jordan, and others scattered from Saul. They had no blacksmith and relied on the Philistines to sharpen farm tools, so only Saul and Jonathan had a sword or spear.

l: Michmash, The First Book of Samuel, Chapter 13
s: Michmash was where two thousand of Saul's men were stationed at the start, and later where the Philistines encamped, east of Beth Aven. The Philistine garrison went out to the pass of Michmash.

l: Gilgal, The First Book of Samuel, Chapter 13
s: Gilgal was where the people gathered after Saul and where Saul waited seven days for Samuel while the people scattered. There Saul offered the burnt offering and was rebuked by Samuel, who then left for Gibeah of Benjamin.

l: burnt offering, The First Book of Samuel, Chapter 13
s: Saul ordered the burnt offering and the peace offerings brought to him at Gilgal and offered the burnt offering himself. Samuel arrived as soon as he had finished.

l: Saul's disobedient offering (Saul's sacrifice at Gilgal), The First Book of Samuel, Chapter 13
s: After waiting seven days, Saul offered the burnt offering because the people were scattering, Samuel had not come, and the Philistines were gathering at Michmash. He said he had not yet sought the LORD's favor and forced himself to do it. Samuel called it foolish, said Saul had not kept the LORD's commandment, and declared that his kingdom would not continue.

l: The First Book of Samuel, The First Book of Samuel, Chapter 14
s: Jonathan son of Saul secretly goes with his armor bearer to attack a Philistine garrison, trusting that the LORD can save by many or by few, and they kill about twenty men. Panic spreads through the Philistine camp, and Saul and his people join the battle as the Philistines strike each other with swords while Hebrews who had been with the Philistines and hidden Israelites turn against them. Saul's oath forbidding food until evening leaves the people faint; Jonathan, unaware of it, eats honey, and the weary people afterward eat meat with the blood, so Saul builds his first altar to the LORD. When God does not answer Saul's inquiry about pursuing the Philistines, lots identify Jonathan as the offender, and Saul declares he must die, but the people rescue him. The chapter ends with a summary of Saul's wars against surrounding enemies, his family, and his army captain Abner.

l: Jonathan, The First Book of Samuel, Chapter 14
s: Jonathan secretly goes with his armor bearer to attack the Philistine garrison, setting a sign and climbing up to kill the men there, which starts the panic. Unaware of his father's oath, he eats honey and is later picked by lot as the offender, and Saul says he must die. The people rescue him, saying he worked with God that day.

l: Saul, The First Book of Samuel, Chapter 14
s: Saul stays at Gibeah with about six hundred men, discovers Jonathan is missing, and then joins the battle. He swears the oath against eating, which leaves his people faint, builds his first altar to the LORD, and, when God gives no answer, uses lots to find the offender and condemns his son Jonathan before the people rescue him. His wars against many enemies, his family, and his habit of taking in valiant men are also described.

l: armor bearer (Jonathan's armor bearer), The First Book of Samuel, Chapter 14
s: The armor bearer tells Jonathan to do all that is in his heart and says he is with him. He follows Jonathan up the crag and kills the Philistines who fall before Jonathan.

l: Philistines, The First Book of Samuel, Chapter 14
s: The Philistines taunt Jonathan and his armor bearer, inviting them up, and about twenty of them are killed. Their camp, garrison and raiders tremble, they strike each other with swords in confusion, and they flee. Israel pursues them from Michmash to Aijalon, and they finally go to their own place; the war against them lasts all the days of Saul.

l: Israel, The First Book of Samuel, Chapter 14
s: Israel is saved by the LORD that day as the battle passes over by Beth Aven, and Hebrews with the Philistines and Israelites hiding in Ephraim join the pursuit. The men of Israel are distressed by Saul's oath, and the people then sin by eating meat with blood before Saul corrects it. The people refuse to let Jonathan die.

l: LORD, The First Book of Samuel, Chapter 14
s: The LORD is trusted by Jonathan to work for them, since nothing restrains him from saving by many or by few, and the text says he saved Israel that day. He does not answer Saul's inquiry about pursuing the Philistines that day, which leads Saul to seek the sin.

l: Saul's army (the people with Saul), The First Book of Samuel, Chapter 14
s: About six hundred men are with Saul and do not know Jonathan has gone. They come to the battle, keep the oath and grow faint, then pounce on the plunder and eat meat with blood, and bring their oxen and sheep to be killed properly. They refuse to let Saul put Jonathan to death and rescue him.

l: honey, The First Book of Samuel, Chapter 14
s: Honey on the ground in the forest is left untouched by the people because of the oath. Jonathan dips his rod in it and eats, and his eyes brighten, which exposes his breaking of the oath and leads to the lot falling on him.

l: Saul's oath, The First Book of Samuel, Chapter 14
s: Saul adjures the people with a curse on anyone who eats before evening and before he is avenged on his enemies. It leaves the people distressed and faint, and Jonathan breaks it unknowingly by eating honey. Jonathan criticizes it as troubling the land, and the people prevent its penalty from being carried out on him.

l: battle against the Philistines at Michmash, The First Book of Samuel, Chapter 14
s: The battle begins with Jonathan and his armor bearer killing about twenty men, followed by trembling, an earthquake and confusion in the Philistine camp. Saul and his people join in, and Hebrews with the Philistines and hidden Israelites turn to help. The Philistines are struck from Michmash to Aijalon and flee, and the LORD saves Israel that day.

l: The First Book of Samuel, The First Book of Samuel, Chapter 15
s: Samuel tells Saul that the LORD commands him to utterly destroy Amalek, including all people and livestock. Saul gathers an army, warns the Kenites to leave, and defeats the Amalekites, but he and the people spare King Agag and the best of the animals. The LORD grieves that he made Saul king, and Samuel confronts Saul, who blames the people and says the animals were for sacrifice. Samuel declares that obedience is better than sacrifice and that the LORD has rejected Saul as king; Saul confesses, tears Samuel's robe, and Samuel says the kingdom is torn from him and given to a better neighbor. Samuel then kills Agag at Gilgal, and he and Saul part for good, with Samuel mourning and the LORD grieving over Saul's kingship.

l: Samuel, The First Book of Samuel, Chapter 15
s: Samuel relays the LORD's command to Saul to destroy Amalek, then cries to the LORD all night after hearing that Saul has been rejected. He confronts Saul at Gilgal, declares that obedience is better than sacrifice, and announces that the kingdom is torn from Saul. He cuts Agag in pieces before the LORD, goes to Ramah, and never sees Saul again before Saul's death, though he mourns for him.

l: Saul, The First Book of Samuel, Chapter 15
s: Saul musters 200,000 footmen and 10,000 men of Judah, spares the Kenites, and strikes the Amalekites, but keeps Agag alive and spares the best livestock. He claims to have obeyed, blames the people, then confesses and begs Samuel to honor him before the elders. He is told he is rejected as king, tears Samuel's robe in grasping it, worships the LORD, and returns to Gibeah.

l: LORD, The First Book of Samuel, Chapter 15
s: The LORD commands the total destruction of Amalek, remembering what Amalek did to Israel on the way out of Egypt. He tells Samuel that he regrets making Saul king because Saul turned back and did not perform his commandments. He rejects Saul as king, and he is described as the Strength of Israel who will not lie or repent, and who grieves that he made Saul king.

l: Amalek, The First Book of Samuel, Chapter 15
s: Amalek is to be struck and utterly destroyed because of how it set itself against Israel on the way up out of Egypt. Saul strikes the Amalekites from Havilah to Shur and destroys all the people with the sword except King Agag, though the Kenites living among them are warned away and spared.

l: Agag, The First Book of Samuel, Chapter 15
s: Agag, king of the Amalekites, is taken alive by Saul and spared along with the best of the livestock. He comes to Samuel cheerfully, saying the bitterness of death is past. Samuel tells him that as his sword made women childless, so will his mother be childless, and cuts him in pieces before the LORD in Gilgal.

l: Israel, The First Book of Samuel, Chapter 15
s: Israel is the people on whose behalf the LORD remembers Amalek's opposition during the exodus from Egypt. Saul was anointed king over Israel and made head of its tribes, but the LORD rejects him from being king over Israel. Samuel says the LORD has torn the kingdom of Israel from Saul and given it to a better neighbor.

l: people (Saul's army), The First Book of Samuel, Chapter 15
s: The people, Saul's army, join Saul in sparing Agag and the best of the livestock while destroying only what was vile and refuse. Saul blames them for taking the plunder to sacrifice at Gilgal, and later says he feared the people and obeyed their voice.

l: plunder (Amalekite livestock spared), The First Book of Samuel, Chapter 15
s: The best of the sheep, cattle, fat calves, lambs and all that was good are kept rather than destroyed, while only the worthless animals are destroyed. Samuel exposes it by the bleating and lowing he hears. Saul claims the animals were kept to sacrifice to the LORD at Gilgal, but Samuel calls taking the plunder evil in the LORD's sight.

l: Saul's disobedience and rejection as king, The First Book of Samuel, Chapter 15
s: Saul's failure to destroy everything as commanded is the LORD's grounds for rejecting him as king. Samuel calls rebellion like witchcraft and stubbornness like idolatry, and says that because Saul rejected the LORD's word, the LORD rejected him. Saul's confession and plea do not reverse it, and the torn robe symbolizes the kingdom being torn from him.

l: The First Book of Samuel, The First Book of Samuel, Chapter 16
s: The LORD tells Samuel to stop mourning for the rejected Saul and to go to Jesse of Bethlehem, where he has provided a king among Jesse's sons. Samuel, fearing Saul, goes under the pretext of a sacrifice, and the LORD rejects Eliab and the other six sons presented, saying he looks at the heart rather than outward appearance. Samuel has the youngest son, David, brought from the sheep, and anoints him in front of his brothers, after which the LORD's Spirit comes mightily on David. Meanwhile the LORD's Spirit departs from Saul and an evil spirit troubles him, so his servants recommend a harp player and one of them names David. David comes to Saul, becomes his armor bearer, and his playing refreshes Saul and drives the evil spirit away.

l: LORD, The First Book of Samuel, Chapter 16
s: The LORD tells Samuel to go to Jesse the Bethlehemite because he has provided a king among Jesse's sons, and he rejects Eliab, stating that he looks at the heart rather than outward appearance. He identifies David as the one to anoint, and his Spirit comes mightily on David while departing from Saul, with an evil spirit from the LORD troubling Saul.

l: Samuel, The First Book of Samuel, Chapter 16
s: Samuel is told to stop mourning for Saul and, fearing Saul will kill him, follows the LORD's instruction to take a heifer and say he has come to sacrifice. He goes to Bethlehem, sanctifies Jesse and his sons, wrongly assumes Eliab is the anointed one, and then anoints David on the LORD's word before returning to Ramah.

l: Saul, The First Book of Samuel, Chapter 16
s: Saul is the king the LORD has rejected, and Samuel fears he would kill him if he learned of the mission. The LORD's Spirit departs from him and an evil spirit troubles him, so he asks his servants for a skilled player and summons David, who becomes his armor bearer, finds favor in his sight, and relieves him with harp playing.

l: Jesse, The First Book of Samuel, Chapter 16
s: Jesse, a Bethlehemite, is called with his sons to the sacrifice and has seven of them pass before Samuel, none of whom the LORD has chosen. He then reveals the youngest, David, is keeping the sheep, sends for him, and later sends David to Saul with a donkey loaded with bread, wine, and a young goat.

l: David, The First Book of Samuel, Chapter 16
s: David is Jesse's youngest son, found keeping the sheep, and is described as ruddy with a handsome face and good appearance. Samuel anoints him among his brothers and the LORD's Spirit comes mightily on him. A young man describes him as a skillful harp player, a mighty man of valor, a man of war, and prudent in speech, and he enters Saul's service as armor bearer, playing the harp to refresh Saul.

l: evil spirit, The First Book of Samuel, Chapter 16
s: An evil spirit from the LORD (called an evil spirit from God by Saul's servants) troubles Saul after the LORD's Spirit leaves him. It departs from him whenever David plays the harp, leaving Saul refreshed and well.

l: anointing of David, The First Book of Samuel, Chapter 16
s: Samuel anoints David with oil from a horn in the middle of his brothers, after the LORD rejects the other seven sons and says, "Arise! Anoint him, for this is he." From that day forward the LORD's Spirit comes mightily on David.

l: The First Book of Samuel, The First Book of Samuel, Chapter 17
s: The Philistines and Saul's Israelite army face each other across the valley of Elah, where the Philistine champion Goliath of Gath, a heavily armed giant, challenges Israel to send a man to fight him, and Saul and all Israel are dismayed. David, the youngest son of Jesse of Bethlehem, brings provisions to his brothers at the camp, hears Goliath's challenge, and is rebuked by his eldest brother Eliab. David volunteers before Saul, citing how he killed a lion and a bear while keeping sheep, refuses Saul's armor, and goes out with his staff, five smooth stones, and a sling. He kills Goliath with a stone to the forehead, cuts off his head with Goliath's own sword, and the Philistines flee and are pursued by Israel and Judah. Saul then asks Abner whose son David is, and David answers that he is the son of Jesse the Bethlehemite.

l: David, The First Book of Samuel, Chapter 17
s: David, the youngest son of Jesse of Bethlehem, brings food to his brothers at the camp, hears Goliath's challenge, and volunteers to fight him despite Saul's doubts and Eliab's anger. He cites killing a lion and a bear, trusts the LORD to deliver him, refuses Saul's armor, and kills Goliath with a sling and stone, then beheads him with Goliath's sword. He brings the head to Jerusalem, puts the armor in his tent, and tells Saul he is the son of Jesse the Bethlehemite.

l: Goliath the Philistine, The First Book of Samuel, Chapter 17
s: Goliath of Gath is a Philistine champion six cubits and a span tall, armed with a bronze helmet, coat of mail, shin armor, javelin, and a spear with an iron head of six hundred shekels. He challenges Israel for forty days to send a man to fight, with the loser's side becoming servants, and he curses and disdains David. David strikes him in the forehead with a stone, and then kills and beheads him with his own sword.

l: Saul, The First Book of Samuel, Chapter 17
s: Saul camps with Israel in the valley of Elah and is dismayed and greatly afraid at Goliath's challenge. He sends for David, doubts that a youth can fight Goliath, then says 'Go! The LORD will be with you' and dresses David in his own armor, which David removes. After the victory he asks Abner whose son David is and is told by David that he is the son of Jesse the Bethlehemite.

l: Philistines, The First Book of Samuel, Chapter 17
s: The Philistines gather their armies at Socoh and encamp between Socoh and Azekah, standing on one mountain facing Israel across the valley. When they see their champion Goliath dead, they flee, and Israel and Judah pursue them to Gai and the gates of Ekron, with the wounded falling on the way to Shaaraim, Gath and Ekron. Israel then plunders their camp.

l: Israel, The First Book of Samuel, Chapter 17
s: Israel's army under Saul stands on the opposite mountain from the Philistines, and its men flee and are terrified when Goliath appears. After David kills Goliath, the men of Israel and of Judah shout, pursue the fleeing Philistines, and plunder their camp.

l: LORD, The First Book of Samuel, Chapter 17
s: David calls the LORD the living God and the LORD of Armies, the God of the armies of Israel, whom Goliath has defied. David says the LORD delivered him from the lion and the bear and will deliver him from Goliath, and that the LORD does not save with sword and spear, for the battle is the LORD's.

l: valley of Elah, The First Book of Samuel, Chapter 17
s: The valley of Elah is where Saul and the men of Israel encamp and set the battle in array against the Philistines. The Philistines stand on one mountain and Israel on the other, with the valley between them, and it is where David kills Goliath.

l: sling and stone, The First Book of Samuel, Chapter 17
s: David chooses five smooth stones from the brook, puts them in his shepherd's bag, and carries his sling in his hand. He slings one stone, which sinks into Goliath's forehead and fells him, so that David prevails with a sling and a stone without a sword in his hand.

l: battle between David and Goliath, The First Book of Samuel, Chapter 17
s: Goliath advances toward David with his shield bearer before him, curses David by his gods, and threatens to give his flesh to the birds and animals. David answers that he comes in the name of the LORD of Armies, runs toward the army to meet him, and fells him with one stone. David then stands over Goliath, draws Goliath's sword, and cuts off his head, causing the Philistines to flee.

l: The First Book of Samuel, The First Book of Samuel, Chapter 18
s: Jonathan bonds with David in covenant, giving him his robe, sword, bow, and sash, while Saul keeps David at his court and sets him over the men of war. When women sing that Saul has slain thousands and David ten thousands, Saul grows angry and jealous, and twice tries to pin David to the wall with his spear. Afraid because the LORD is with David, Saul makes him captain of a thousand, offers him Merab and then Michal in marriage, and sets a dowry of one hundred Philistine foreskins hoping the Philistines will kill him. David instead kills two hundred Philistines, delivers the foreskins, and marries Michal. Saul becomes David's continual enemy as David's name grows highly esteemed.

l: Saul, The First Book of Samuel, Chapter 18
s: Saul keeps David with him and sets him over the men of war, but becomes angry and suspicious after the women's song credits David with ten thousands. He twice throws his spear at David, fears him because the LORD has left Saul, and makes him a captain of a thousand. He offers Merab and then Michal in hopes the Philistines will kill David, demands a hundred foreskins as dowry, and ends the chapter as David's continual enemy.

l: David, The First Book of Samuel, Chapter 18
s: David serves wherever Saul sends him, behaves wisely, and is set over the men of war, winning the favor of the people and Saul's servants. He escapes Saul's spear twice, is made captain of a thousand, and humbly deflects the offers of marriage to the king's daughter. He kills two hundred Philistines, brings their foreskins, and marries Michal, and his name is highly esteemed.

l: Jonathan, The First Book of Samuel, Chapter 18
s: Jonathan's soul is knit with David's, and he loves David as his own soul. He makes a covenant with David and gives him his robe, clothing, sword, bow, and sash.

l: Michal, The First Book of Samuel, Chapter 18
s: Michal, Saul's daughter, loves David, and Saul is pleased by this because he intends her to be a snare for David. After David delivers the dowry, Saul gives her to him as wife.

l: LORD, The First Book of Samuel, Chapter 18
s: The LORD is with David and has departed from Saul, which makes Saul afraid. An evil spirit from God comes mightily on Saul, and Saul recognizes that the LORD is with David.

l: Philistines, The First Book of Samuel, Chapter 18
s: The Philistines are the enemy whose hand Saul hopes will fall on David, both in battle and in the dowry scheme. David kills two hundred of them to meet the dowry, and he continues to act more wisely than Saul's servants whenever their princes go out to fight.

l: dowry of one hundred Philistine foreskins, The First Book of Samuel, Chapter 18
s: Saul demands this as the only dowry for Michal, claiming it is to avenge the king's enemies, but actually hoping David will fall by the Philistines' hand. David doubles it, bringing the foreskins of two hundred men in full number to the king, and so wins Michal as wife.

l: The First Book of Samuel, The First Book of Samuel, Chapter 19
s: Saul orders his son Jonathan and his servants to kill David, but Jonathan warns David to hide and then persuades Saul to swear that David will not be put to death. After David wins another battle against the Philistines, an evil spirit comes on Saul and he tries to pin David to the wall with a spear; David escapes. Saul sends messengers to David's house, and Michal lowers David through a window and deceives the messengers with a teraphim in the bed, then tells Saul that David threatened her. David flees to Samuel at Ramah and lives with him in Naioth, where Saul's three groups of messengers are overcome by God's Spirit and prophesy. Saul himself goes to Naioth, prophesies, strips off his clothes, and lies naked all day and night, which gives rise to the saying, "Is Saul also among the prophets?"

l: Saul, The First Book of Samuel, Chapter 19
s: Saul orders David killed, then swears at Jonathan's urging that David will not die, but an evil spirit from the LORD comes on him and he throws his spear at David. He sends messengers to David's house and later to Naioth to seize him, and finally goes there himself, where God's Spirit overcomes him and he prophesies and lies naked a day and a night.

l: Jonathan, The First Book of Samuel, Chapter 19
s: Jonathan, who greatly delights in David, warns him of Saul's plan and tells him to hide. He speaks well of David to Saul, argues that David has not sinned and that killing him would be shedding innocent blood, and brings David back into Saul's presence after Saul swears not to kill him.

l: David, The First Book of Samuel, Chapter 19
s: David fights the Philistines and defeats them with great slaughter, then escapes Saul's spear while playing music. Michal lets him down through a window to escape the messengers at his house, and he flees to Samuel at Ramah, tells him all Saul has done, and lives with him in Naioth.

l: Michal, The First Book of Samuel, Chapter 19
s: Michal, David's wife, warns David that he will be killed in the morning unless he flees, and lets him down through the window. She places the teraphim in the bed to deceive Saul's messengers, claims David is sick, and when Saul confronts her says David told her, "Let me go! Why should I kill you?"

l: Samuel, The First Book of Samuel, Chapter 19
s: David comes to Samuel at Ramah and tells him all that Saul has done, and the two go to live in Naioth. When Saul's messengers arrive, Samuel is seen standing as head over the company of the prophets who are prophesying.

l: messengers (Saul's messengers), The First Book of Samuel, Chapter 19
s: Saul sends messengers to watch David's house and kill him in the morning, but Michal says he is sick and they find only the teraphim in the bed. Saul later sends three successive groups of messengers to seize David at Naioth, and each group is overcome by God's Spirit and prophesies instead.

l: company of the prophets, The First Book of Samuel, Chapter 19
s: The company of the prophets is seen prophesying at Naioth with Samuel standing as head over them. Saul's messengers who come to seize David join in the prophesying when God's Spirit comes on them.

l: teraphim (Michal's decoy in David's bed), The First Book of Samuel, Chapter 19
s: Michal lays the teraphim in David's bed, puts a pillow of goats' hair at its head, and covers it with clothes to make it look like a sick man. When Saul's messengers come in, they find the teraphim in the bed instead of David, exposing the deception.

l: Naioth in Ramah, The First Book of Samuel, Chapter 19
s: Naioth, in Ramah, is where David and Samuel go to live after David's escape. Saul is told David is there, and his messengers and then Saul himself are overcome by God's Spirit and prophesy there.

l: Ramah, The First Book of Samuel, Chapter 19
s: Ramah is where David comes to Samuel after fleeing Saul, and where Naioth is located. Saul goes to Ramah, comes to the great well in Secu, asks where Samuel and David are, and is told they are at Naioth in Ramah.

l: Saul's prophesying and nakedness, The First Book of Samuel, Chapter 19
s: When Saul goes to Naioth, God's Spirit comes on him and he prophesies as he goes. He strips off his clothes, prophesies before Samuel, and lies naked all that day and night, which gives rise to the saying, "Is Saul also among the prophets?"

l: The First Book of Samuel, The First Book of Samuel, Chapter 20
s: David flees from Naioth in Ramah and asks Jonathan what he has done to make Saul seek his life; Jonathan doubts it, but David swears there is only a step between him and death. They devise a test: David will hide in the field during the new moon feast, and Jonathan will report Saul's reaction using a signal of three arrows shot beside the stone Ezel. Jonathan and David renew their covenant, and at the feast Saul notices David's empty place, then erupts in anger at Jonathan, insults him, declares David must die, and hurls a spear at him. Jonathan, grieved and angry, shoots the arrows beyond his boy as the agreed warning, sends the boy to the city, and he and David weep, kiss, and part in peace, reaffirming their oath in the LORD's name.

l: David, The First Book of Samuel, Chapter 20
s: David flees from Naioth in Ramah and protests to Jonathan his innocence, swearing there is but a step between him and death. He hides in the field during the new moon feast, receives the arrow signal that he must go away, and then comes out from the south, bows three times, and weeps with Jonathan before departing.

l: Jonathan, The First Book of Samuel, Chapter 20
s: Jonathan first doubts that his father wants David dead, then promises to help, makes a covenant with David's house, and arranges the arrow signal. After Saul rages at him and throws a spear, Jonathan knows David is doomed, eats nothing that day in grief, carries out the signal, and parts from David with an oath of peace.

l: Saul, The First Book of Samuel, Chapter 20
s: Saul sits at the new moon feast, says nothing on the first day of David's absence because he thinks David is unclean, and on the second day asks why the son of Jesse has not come. On hearing Jonathan's excuse he burns with anger, insults Jonathan, declares David shall surely die, and casts his spear at his own son.

l: LORD, The First Book of Samuel, Chapter 20
s: The LORD is invoked repeatedly as witness to oaths between David and Jonathan, and Jonathan says the LORD is between them forever and between their offspring. Jonathan also reads the signal of the arrows beyond the boy as the LORD sending David away.

l: boy (Jonathan's boy), The First Book of Samuel, Chapter 20
s: Jonathan's boy goes with him to the field and runs to find the arrows Jonathan shoots, while Jonathan shouts after him to hurry. He understands nothing of the signal, as only Jonathan and David know the matter, and he is sent back to the city carrying Jonathan's weapons.

l: covenant (between Jonathan and David), The First Book of Samuel, Chapter 20
s: David appeals to the covenant of the LORD that Jonathan brought him into, and Jonathan renews it with David's house, asking that David show kindness to his house forever. At parting they again affirm that the LORD is between them and between their offspring forever.

l: arrows (Jonathan's arrows), The First Book of Samuel, Chapter 20
s: Jonathan plans to shoot three arrows by the stone Ezel as a secret signal: arrows on this side of the boy mean peace, arrows beyond him mean David must go. Jonathan shoots an arrow beyond the boy and calls out that it is beyond him, confirming the danger to David.

l: new moon feast (Saul's table), The First Book of Samuel, Chapter 20
s: The new moon feast is the occasion David says he should attend and the test of Saul's intentions. David's seat is empty on both days, which leads to Saul's questioning, his outburst against Jonathan, and the throwing of his spear, after which Jonathan leaves the table in fierce anger.

l: The First Book of Samuel, The First Book of Samuel, Chapter 21
s: David comes alone to Nob and tells the priest Ahimelech that the king has sent him on secret business, asking for bread. Ahimelech gives him the holy show bread after David assures him that the young men have kept themselves from women, and Doeg the Edomite, a servant of Saul, is present and detained before the LORD. David also asks for a weapon and receives the sword of Goliath, which is wrapped in a cloth behind the ephod. David then flees from Saul to Achish, king of Gath, where the servants of Achish recall the song about Saul's thousands and David's ten thousands. Afraid, David pretends to be insane by scribbling on the gate doors and letting spittle run down his beard, and Achish, disgusted, dismisses him.

l: David, The First Book of Samuel, Chapter 21
s: David came alone to Nob and told Ahimelech that the king had sent him on secret business, then obtained the holy bread and Goliath's sword. He fled that day for fear of Saul to Achish of Gath, where he was recognized and became very afraid. He feigned madness to escape harm.

l: Ahimelech, The First Book of Samuel, Chapter 21
s: Ahimelech the priest met David trembling and questioned why he was alone. He gave David the holy bread after hearing that the young men were kept from women, and he told David that Goliath's sword was there and gave it to him.

l: Saul, The First Book of Samuel, Chapter 21
s: Saul is called the king in David's account of secret business, and David fled for fear of him. One of his servants, Doeg the Edomite, the best of his herdsmen, was at Nob that day. The servants of Achish recall a song that Saul has slain his thousands and David his ten thousands.

l: holy bread, The First Book of Samuel, Chapter 21
s: Ahimelech said he had no common bread, only holy bread, which could be given only if the young men had kept themselves from women. After David's assurance, the priest gave it to him, since the only bread there was the show bread taken from before the LORD to be replaced with hot bread.

l: sword of Goliath, The First Book of Samuel, Chapter 21
s: The sword of Goliath the Philistine, whom David killed in the valley of Elah, was kept wrapped in a cloth behind the ephod at Nob. Ahimelech said it was the only weapon there, and David said there was none like it and took it.

l: Achish, The First Book of Samuel, Chapter 21
s: Achish is the king of Gath, to whom David fled. His servants identified David as the king of the land and recalled the song about him. Seeing David act insane, Achish rebuked his servants for bringing a madman and refused to let him into his house.

l: David's feigned insanity, The First Book of Samuel, Chapter 21
s: Fearing Achish after his servants recognized him, David changed his behavior, scribbled on the doors of the gate, and let spittle fall on his beard. Achish was convinced he was a madman and wanted nothing to do with him.

l: The First Book of Samuel, The First Book of Samuel, Chapter 22
s: David flees to Adullam's cave, where his brothers, his father's house, and about four hundred distressed, indebted, and discontented men gather to him as captain. He takes his parents to the king of Moab for safekeeping, and the prophet Gad then tells him to leave the stronghold for the land of Judah, so he goes to the forest of Hereth. Saul, learning David has been found, accuses his Benjamite servants of conspiracy, and Doeg the Edomite reports that David came to Ahimelech at Nob, who inquired of the LORD for him and gave him food and Goliath's sword. Saul summons Ahimelech and the priests, rejects Ahimelech's defense, and condemns them to death; when his guards refuse, Doeg kills eighty-five priests and destroys Nob with its people and animals. Abiathar, one of Ahimelech's sons, escapes to David, who admits responsibility and promises him safety.

l: David, The First Book of Samuel, Chapter 22
s: David escaped to Adullam's cave, became captain over about four hundred men, and placed his parents with the king of Moab. Following Gad's instruction he went to the forest of Hereth. When Abiathar reported the killings at Nob, David said he had known Doeg would tell Saul, accepted responsibility for the deaths of Abiathar's father's house, and promised Abiathar protection.

l: Saul, The First Book of Samuel, Chapter 22
s: Saul, sitting under the tamarisk tree at Ramah with his spear, accused his servants of conspiring against him with David and his son. He condemned Ahimelech and the priests of Nob to death, and when his guards refused to strike them he ordered Doeg to do it.

l: Ahimelech, The First Book of Samuel, Chapter 22
s: Ahimelech, son of Ahitub and a priest at Nob, was summoned by Saul and accused of conspiring with David by giving him bread and a sword and inquiring of God for him. He defended himself by praising David's faithfulness as the king's son-in-law and claiming he knew nothing of any plot. Saul sentenced him to death along with all his father's house.

l: Doeg the Edomite, The First Book of Samuel, Chapter 22
s: Doeg, standing among Saul's servants, told Saul he had seen David come to Ahimelech at Nob. When Saul's guards refused to kill the priests, Doeg obeyed the order, killing eighty-five linen-ephod-wearing priests and then striking down the city of Nob. David later said he had known Doeg would tell Saul.

l: Abiathar, The First Book of Samuel, Chapter 22
s: Abiathar, a son of Ahimelech son of Ahitub, was the one who escaped the killing at Nob and fled to David. He told David that Saul had slain the LORD's priests, and David promised him safety with him.

l: Nob, The First Book of Samuel, Chapter 22
s: Nob is the city of the priests, where Ahimelech lived and where David had received food and Goliath's sword. Doeg struck it with the sword, killing men, women, children, nursing babies, and its cattle, donkeys, and sheep.

l: David's four hundred men, The First Book of Samuel, Chapter 22
s: About four hundred men, everyone in distress, in debt, or discontented, gathered to David at Adullam's cave, and he became their captain. His brothers and his father's house also came down to join him there.

l: priests of Nob, The First Book of Samuel, Chapter 22
s: Saul summoned Ahimelech and all his father's house, the priests at Nob, and condemned them for allegedly aiding David. The king's servants refused to raise a hand against these priests of the LORD, but Doeg killed eighty-five of them. Only Abiathar escaped.

l: massacre of Nob, The First Book of Samuel, Chapter 22
s: On the day Saul condemned the priests, Doeg killed eighty-five linen-ephod-wearing priests and struck Nob with the sword, killing men, women, children, nursing babies, and livestock. Saul's own servants refused to carry out the order, and only Abiathar escaped, fleeing to David, who accepted responsibility for the deaths.

l: The First Book of Samuel, The First Book of Samuel, Chapter 23
s: David learns that the Philistines are attacking Keilah, inquires of the LORD, and with his men saves the town, after which Abiathar the son of Ahimelech comes to him with an ephod. Saul hears David is in Keilah and summons the people to besiege him, but the LORD tells David that Saul will come and that the men of Keilah would deliver him up, so David and his roughly six hundred men leave. David stays in the wilderness of Ziph, where Jonathan comes to strengthen him and they make a covenant before the LORD. The Ziphites inform Saul of David's hiding place, and Saul pursues him into the wilderness of Maon, nearly surrounding him, until a messenger reports a Philistine raid and Saul turns back, after which David goes to the strongholds of En Gedi.

l: David, The First Book of Samuel, Chapter 23
s: David inquires of the LORD twice, saves Keilah from the Philistines, then inquires again and learns that Saul will come and that the men of Keilah would deliver him up, so he leaves with his men. He hides in the wilderness of Ziph and then Maon, makes a covenant with Jonathan, narrowly escapes Saul when the Philistines raid, and goes up to the strongholds of En Gedi.

l: Saul, The First Book of Samuel, Chapter 23
s: Saul summons the people to besiege David at Keilah, believing God has delivered him into his hand, but abandons the effort when told David has escaped. He seeks David daily, accepts the Ziphites' offer to deliver him up, and pursues him in the wilderness of Maon until a messenger reports a Philistine raid and he turns back.

l: Jonathan, The First Book of Samuel, Chapter 23
s: Jonathan goes to David in the woods and strengthens his hand in God. He tells David that Saul will not find him, that David will be king over Israel with Jonathan next to him, and that Saul knows this too; the two make a covenant before the LORD and Jonathan returns home.

l: LORD, The First Book of Samuel, Chapter 23
s: The LORD answers David's inquiries, telling him to strike the Philistines and save Keilah and promising to deliver them into his hand. He also reveals that Saul will come down and that the men of Keilah will deliver David up, and he does not deliver David into Saul's hand.

l: Philistines, The First Book of Samuel, Chapter 23
s: The Philistines fight against Keilah and rob its threshing floors, and David and his men defeat them with a great slaughter and take their livestock. Later a Philistine raid on the land draws Saul away from pursuing David.

l: Keilah, The First Book of Samuel, Chapter 23
s: Keilah is attacked by the Philistines and saved by David and his men. Saul plans to besiege David there, and the LORD says its men would deliver David up, so David leaves.

l: David's men, The First Book of Samuel, Chapter 23
s: David's men voice fear about going to Keilah against the Philistines, but go with David, fight, and save the inhabitants. About six hundred of them leave Keilah with David and later are with him in the wilderness of Maon when Saul nearly surrounds them.

l: Ziphites, The First Book of Samuel, Chapter 23
s: The Ziphites go to Saul at Gibeah and report that David is hiding in the strongholds in the woods of the hill of Hachilah, offering to deliver him up. Saul blesses them for their compassion and sends them to learn David's hiding places more certainly.

l: wilderness of Ziph, The First Book of Samuel, Chapter 23
s: David stays in the strongholds and woods of the wilderness of Ziph while Saul seeks him daily. Jonathan visits him there and they make a covenant.

l: wilderness of Maon, The First Book of Samuel, Chapter 23
s: David and his men move to the wilderness of Maon, in the Arabah south of the desert, when Saul comes seeking him. Saul pursues him there and nearly surrounds him on the mountain until the Philistine raid calls Saul away, and the place is named Sela Hammahlekoth.

l: The First Book of Samuel, The First Book of Samuel, Chapter 24
s: Saul takes three thousand chosen men to hunt David in the wilderness of En Gedi, and goes into a cave to relieve himself, where David and his men are hiding. David's men urge him to seize the chance, but David only cuts off the skirt of Saul's robe and then stops his men from attacking, because Saul is the LORD's anointed. David calls after Saul, shows him the skirt as proof he spared him, and asks the LORD to judge between them. Saul weeps, admits David is more righteous, acknowledges that David will be king, and makes David swear not to cut off his offspring or destroy his name. David swears, Saul goes home, and David and his men go up to the stronghold.

l: Saul, The First Book of Samuel, Chapter 24
s: Saul, told that David is in the wilderness of En Gedi, takes three thousand chosen men to seek him and enters a cave to relieve himself, unaware David is inside. After David spares him and shows him the skirt, Saul weeps, calls David more righteous than himself, and says he knows David will surely be king. He makes David swear not to cut off his offspring or destroy his name, then goes home.

l: David, The First Book of Samuel, Chapter 24
s: David, hiding in the innermost parts of the cave, secretly cuts off the skirt of Saul's robe but is struck in his heart and restrains his men from harming Saul, since Saul is the LORD's anointed. He then calls out to Saul, bows, shows the skirt as proof of his innocence, and asks the LORD to judge between them. He swears to Saul not to cut off his offspring and goes up to the stronghold with his men.

l: LORD, The First Book of Samuel, Chapter 24
s: The LORD is invoked by David's men as having said he would deliver David's enemy into his hand, and David says the LORD delivered Saul into his hand in the cave. David appeals to the LORD as judge and avenger between him and Saul, and Saul asks the LORD to reward David with good. Saul is called the LORD's anointed, which is David's reason for refusing to harm him.

l: David's men, The First Book of Samuel, Chapter 24
s: David's men are staying with him in the innermost parts of the cave and urge him to act on the day the LORD spoke of, when his enemy is delivered into his hand. David checks them with his words and does not allow them to rise against Saul. They later go up to the stronghold with David.

l: cave (near the sheep pens), The First Book of Samuel, Chapter 24
s: The cave by the sheep pens is where Saul goes in to relieve himself while David and his men stay in its innermost parts. It is the place where David cuts off Saul's skirt and spares his life. Saul leaves the cave and goes on his way, and David follows afterward.

l: skirt of Saul's robe, The First Book of Samuel, Chapter 24
s: David secretly cuts off the skirt of Saul's robe in the cave, and his heart strikes him afterward for doing so. He holds it up to Saul as proof that he had the chance to kill him and did not, showing there is neither evil nor disobedience in his hand.

l: The First Book of Samuel, The First Book of Samuel, Chapter 25
s: After Samuel dies and is mourned, David goes down to the wilderness of Paran and sends ten young men to ask the wealthy, surly Nabal of Maon for provisions during his sheep-shearing. Nabal insults David and refuses, so David arms about four hundred men and swears to kill every male of Nabal's house. Nabal's wife Abigail, warned by one of Nabal's young men, secretly brings a large gift of food to David, takes the blame on herself, and persuades him not to shed blood or avenge himself. She tells Nabal nothing until morning because he is drunk, and when he hears he becomes as a stone and dies about ten days later when the LORD strikes him. David praises the LORD, then sends for Abigail and she becomes his wife, along with Ahinoam of Jezreel, while Saul has given David's wife Michal to Palti.

l: David, The First Book of Samuel, Chapter 25
s: David sends ten young men to Nabal to request provisions, and when Nabal insults them he arms four hundred men and vows to kill every male of Nabal's house. Abigail's plea turns him back, and he blesses the LORD and her discretion for keeping him from blood guiltiness. After Nabal dies, David takes Abigail as his wife, and also takes Ahinoam of Jezreel, while Saul has given his wife Michal to Palti.

l: Abigail, The First Book of Samuel, Chapter 25
s: Abigail, Nabal's intelligent and beautiful wife, acts quickly on a young man's warning, loading donkeys with food and secretly riding out to meet David. She bows before him, takes the blame, and speaks of the LORD making David a sure house and prince over Israel, which turns him from vengeance. She tells Nabal only in the morning, and after his death she humbly accepts David's proposal and becomes his wife.

l: Nabal, The First Book of Samuel, Chapter 25
s: Nabal is a very wealthy man of the house of Caleb with three thousand sheep and a thousand goats, described as surly and evil in his doings. He scorns David's request, holds a kingly feast and gets drunk, and when told of the danger in the morning his heart dies within him and he becomes as a stone. About ten days later the LORD strikes him and he dies.

l: LORD, The First Book of Samuel, Chapter 25
s: The LORD is invoked by Abigail as having withheld David from blood guiltiness and as the one who will make David's house sure and appoint him prince over Israel. David credits the LORD with sending Abigail to meet him. The LORD strikes Nabal so that he dies, and David says the LORD pleaded his cause and returned Nabal's evil on his own head.

l: David's young men, The First Book of Samuel, Chapter 25
s: Ten of David's young men go to Carmel, deliver David's greeting and request to Nabal in his name, and wait, only to be insulted and sent back. A young man of Nabal's later testifies that they were very good to Nabal's shepherds, acting as a wall by night and day. Four hundred of David's men put on swords to follow him while two hundred stay with the baggage, and Abigail's gift is given to them.

l: Abigail's gift, The First Book of Samuel, Chapter 25
s: Abigail gathers two hundred loaves of bread, two containers of wine, five dressed sheep, five seahs of parched grain, one hundred clusters of raisins, and two hundred cakes of figs, and sends them ahead on donkeys without telling Nabal. She asks that it be given to David's young men, and David receives it from her hand and tells her to go up in peace.

l: Nabal's death, The First Book of Samuel, Chapter 25
s: After Nabal learns in the morning what Abigail did, his heart dies within him and he becomes as a stone. About ten days later the LORD strikes him and he dies. David, hearing of it, blesses the LORD for pleading his cause and keeping him from evil, and then sends to take Abigail as his wife.

l: Nabal's insult to David's messengers, The First Book of Samuel, Chapter 25
s: Nabal answers David's servants by asking who David and the son of Jesse are, saying many servants break away from their masters, and refusing to give his bread, water, and meat to men of unknown origin. The messengers return and report this to David, who then orders his men to put on their swords. One of Nabal's young men also tells Abigail that Nabal insulted the messengers even though David's men had protected the shepherds.

l: The First Book of Samuel, The First Book of Samuel, Chapter 26
s: The Ziphites tell Saul that David is hiding in the hill of Hachilah, so Saul goes down to the wilderness of Ziph with three thousand chosen men and camps there. David learns of this through spies and goes by night with Abishai to Saul's camp, where Saul, Abner, and the people lie asleep under a deep sleep from the LORD. Abishai urges David to let him kill Saul with the spear, but David refuses to harm the LORD's anointed and instead takes the spear and the jar of water from Saul's head. From a distant mountaintop David calls out to Abner, rebukes him for failing to guard the king, and shows the spear as proof, and Saul recognizes David's voice. Saul admits he has sinned and played the fool, blesses David, and the two part ways.

l: David, The First Book of Samuel, Chapter 26
s: David learns through spies that Saul has come after him, then goes by night with Abishai into Saul's camp. He refuses to let Abishai kill the sleeping Saul because Saul is the LORD's anointed, takes the spear and water jar instead, and from a distant mountain rebukes Abner and appeals to Saul, who blesses him.

l: Saul, The First Book of Samuel, Chapter 26
s: Saul goes down to the wilderness of Ziph with three thousand chosen men to seek David and sleeps in his camp with his spear stuck in the ground at his head. David spares him, and after hearing David's appeal Saul confesses that he has sinned and played the fool, promises to do David no more harm, and blesses him before returning to his place.

l: Abishai the son of Zeruiah, The First Book of Samuel, Chapter 26
s: Abishai, brother of Joab, volunteers to go down into Saul's camp with David. He urges David to let him strike Saul with the spear in one stroke, but David forbids it.

l: Abner, The First Book of Samuel, Chapter 26
s: Abner, captain of Saul's army, sleeps beside Saul with the people around them while David takes the spear and water jar. David calls to him from a distant mountain and rebukes him for not keeping watch over the king, saying he is worthy to die.

l: LORD, The First Book of Samuel, Chapter 26
s: The LORD sends a deep sleep on Saul's camp so that no one sees or wakes as David takes the spear and jar. David invokes him as the one who will strike Saul in his own time and as the one who gives each man his righteousness and faithfulness, and asks him to deliver David from oppression.

l: spear (Saul's spear), The First Book of Samuel, Chapter 26
s: Saul's spear is stuck in the ground at his head as he sleeps, and Abishai wants to use it to strike him. David instead takes it away, shows it from the mountain as proof of how close he came, and offers to have a young man come over and retrieve it.

l: The First Book of Samuel, The First Book of Samuel, Chapter 27
s: David, fearing he will one day die by Saul's hand, decides to escape to the land of the Philistines and goes with his six hundred men and their households, including his two wives Ahinoam and Abigail, to Achish, king of Gath. When Saul hears David has fled to Gath, he stops searching for him. David asks Achish for a place in the country, and Achish gives him Ziklag, where David lives a full year and four months. David and his men raid the Geshurites, Girzites, and Amalekites, killing every man and woman and taking livestock and clothing. David tells Achish he raided the South of Judah, Jerahmeelites, and Kenites, and Achish believes him, concluding that David has made himself abhorrent to Israel and will be his servant forever.

l: David, The First Book of Samuel, Chapter 27
s: David, believing he will perish by Saul's hand, escapes with his six hundred men and two wives to Achish at Gath, and later asks for and receives Ziklag, living in Philistine country a year and four months. He raids the Geshurites, Girzites, and Amalekites, leaving no man or woman alive, and deceives Achish by claiming he raided Judah's South and the South of the Jerahmeelites and Kenites. He kills all survivors so no one can report his deed.

l: Saul, The First Book of Samuel, Chapter 27
s: Saul is the one David fears will kill him. When told that David has fled to Gath, Saul stops looking for him.

l: Achish, The First Book of Samuel, Chapter 27
s: Achish, son of Maoch and king of Gath, receives David and his household-bearing men, and gives David Ziklag at his request. He believes David's false report of raiding Judah and concludes that Israel abhors David, so David will be his servant forever.

l: David's men, The First Book of Samuel, Chapter 27
s: The six hundred men go with David to Achish at Gath, each with his household, and later live in Ziklag. They go up with David to raid the Geshurites, Girzites, and Amalekites.

l: Ziklag, The First Book of Samuel, Chapter 27
s: Ziklag is given to David by Achish when David asks for a city in the country rather than living in the royal city. The text notes that it belongs to the kings of Judah to this day.

l: David's raid on the Geshurites, Girzites, and Amalekites, The First Book of Samuel, Chapter 27
s: David and his men strike the land of these inhabitants, who live on the way to Shur and Egypt, saving no man or woman alive and taking sheep, cattle, donkeys, camels, and clothing. David then returns to Achish and misrepresents the raid as against the South of Judah, the Jerahmeelites, and the Kenites, killing everyone so none can tell the truth.

l: David's flight to the Philistines, The First Book of Samuel, Chapter 27
s: David decides there is nothing better than escaping to the land of the Philistines, hoping Saul will despair of seeking him in Israel's borders. He crosses over with his six hundred men to Achish of Gath, and Saul stops pursuing him when told.

l: The First Book of Samuel, The First Book of Samuel, Chapter 28
s: The Philistines gather to fight Israel, and Achish tells David he and his men must march with him, promising to make David his bodyguard. Saul, terrified at the Philistine camp at Shunem and unanswered by the LORD through dreams, Urim, or prophets, disguises himself and goes by night with two men to a woman at Endor who has a familiar spirit. After Saul swears she will not be punished, she brings up Samuel, who tells Saul that the LORD has become his adversary, has given the kingdom to David because of Saul's disobedience regarding Amalek, and will deliver Israel and Saul and his sons to the Philistines the next day. Saul collapses from fear and from having eaten nothing, and the woman and his servants persuade him to eat a meal of a fattened calf and unleavened bread before they leave that night.

l: Saul, The First Book of Samuel, Chapter 28
s: Saul, afraid at the sight of the Philistine army and unanswered by the LORD, disguises himself and goes by night to the woman at Endor, swearing by the LORD that she will not be punished, and asks her to bring up Samuel. Samuel tells him that the kingdom is torn from him for disobeying over Amalek and that he and his sons will die with Israel's army defeated the next day. Saul falls down terrified and weak from fasting, refuses food at first, then is persuaded to eat and leaves that night.

l: Samuel, The First Book of Samuel, Chapter 28
s: Samuel is noted as dead and buried in Ramah, mourned by all Israel. Brought up by the woman at Endor, appearing as an old man in a robe, he asks Saul why he has been disturbed, and tells him the LORD has become his adversary, has given the kingdom to David, and will deliver Israel to the Philistines, with Saul and his sons joining Samuel the next day.

l: woman at Endor, The First Book of Samuel, Chapter 28
s: The woman at Endor, who has a familiar spirit, is sought out by the disguised Saul. She fears for her life because Saul had cut off such practitioners, but after he swears an oath she brings up Samuel, and cries out on seeing him, recognizing the visitor as Saul. Afterward she urges the collapsed Saul to eat, kills her fattened calf, and bakes unleavened bread for him and his servants.

l: David, The First Book of Samuel, Chapter 28
s: David is told by Achish that he and his men will go out with the Philistine army. David replies that Achish will know what his servant can do, and Achish promises to make him his bodyguard forever. Samuel also tells Saul that the LORD has given the kingdom to David, here called Saul's neighbor.

l: Philistines, The First Book of Samuel, Chapter 28
s: The Philistines gather their armies to fight Israel and encamp at Shunem, with Achish drafting David and his men to go with him. Their army terrifies Saul, and Samuel prophesies that the LORD will deliver Israel and Saul into their hand.

l: Israel, The First Book of Samuel, Chapter 28
s: All of Israel is said to have mourned and buried Samuel in Ramah. Saul gathers Israel and encamps at Gilboa against the Philistines, and Samuel declares that the LORD will deliver the army of Israel into the Philistines' hand.

l: LORD, The First Book of Samuel, Chapter 28
s: The LORD does not answer Saul by dreams, Urim, or prophets. Through Samuel it is said that the LORD has departed from Saul and become his adversary, has torn the kingdom from him and given it to David because Saul did not obey or execute his wrath on Amalek, and will deliver Israel and Saul to the Philistines. Saul swears an oath to the woman by the LORD's name.

l: Philistine-Israelite war, The First Book of Samuel, Chapter 28
s: The Philistines gather and encamp at Shunem while Saul gathers Israel at Gilboa. Samuel foretells that Israel's army will be delivered into Philistine hands and that Saul and his sons will die the following day.

l: The First Book of Samuel, The First Book of Samuel, Chapter 29
s: The Philistines gather all their armies at Aphek while the Israelites camp by the spring in Jezreel. David and his men march in the rear with Achish, prompting the Philistine princes to ask about these Hebrews. Achish vouches for David's faithfulness, but the princes angrily demand he be sent back, fearing David would turn against them in battle and win his lord's favor with their heads, and they recall the song about Saul's thousands and David's ten thousands. Achish reluctantly tells David to go in peace, and David protests that he has done nothing wrong. David and his men rise early and depart for the land of the Philistines, while the Philistines go up to Jezreel.

l: Philistines, The First Book of Samuel, Chapter 29
s: The Philistines gather all their armies at Aphek, with their lords passing in review by hundreds and thousands. After David's dismissal, they go up to Jezreel, where the Israelites are encamped by the spring.

l: princes of the Philistines, The First Book of Samuel, Chapter 29
s: The princes question the presence of the Hebrews and angrily insist that Achish send David back, fearing he would become an adversary in battle and reconcile himself to his lord with the heads of their men. They cite the song 'Saul has slain his thousands, and David his ten thousands.' Their objection prevails and David is sent away.

l: David, The First Book of Samuel, Chapter 29
s: David marches in the rear with Achish and his men, and is vouched for by Achish but rejected by the Philistine princes. He protests that he has done nothing wrong and asks why he may not fight the enemies of his lord the king. He nonetheless rises early with his men and departs to the land of the Philistines.

l: Achish, The First Book of Samuel, Chapter 29
s: Achish defends David to the princes, saying he has been with him for years and that he has found no fault in him since he fell away. He tells David he is upright and good in his sight, as an angel of God, but yields to the princes and orders him to leave at first light in peace.

l: battle against Israel, The First Book of Samuel, Chapter 29
s: The Philistines assemble at Aphek while the Israelites camp by the spring in Jezreel, setting the stage for battle. The princes refuse to let David go into it with them for fear he would turn against them. At the end of the unit the Philistines go up to Jezreel.

l: The First Book of Samuel, The First Book of Samuel, Chapter 30
s: David and his men return to Ziklag on the third day to find it burned by the Amalekites, who had taken their wives, sons, and daughters captive. The grieving men talk of stoning David, but he strengthens himself in the LORD, has Abiathar the priest bring the ephod, and inquires of the LORD, who tells him to pursue and he will recover all. Of the six hundred men, two hundred are too faint to cross the brook Besor, so David presses on with four hundred, and an Egyptian servant abandoned by the Amalekites leads them to the raiders' camp. David strikes the Amalekites from twilight until the evening of the next day, with only four hundred young men on camels escaping, and recovers everything and everyone taken. When wicked men among his company refuse to share the plunder with the two hundred who stayed behind, David rules that all shall share alike, makes it a statute for Israel, and sends gifts from the plunder to the elders of Judah and to many towns.

l: David, The First Book of Samuel, Chapter 30
s: David finds Ziklag burned and his two wives, Ahinoam and Abigail, taken captive. Though his men speak of stoning him, he strengthens himself in the LORD, inquires through the ephod, pursues the Amalekites, and recovers everything. He rules that those who stayed with the baggage share equally with those who fought, and sends gifts from the plunder to the elders of Judah and to friends in many towns.

l: David's men, The First Book of Samuel, Chapter 30
s: The six hundred men weep until they have no strength when they find Ziklag burned and their families taken, and in their grief speak of stoning David. Four hundred cross the brook Besor and pursue the Amalekites to victory, recovering their families and goods. Some among them argue against sharing the plunder with those left behind, but David overrules them.

l: Ziklag, The First Book of Samuel, Chapter 30
s: Ziklag is struck and burned with fire by the Amalekites, who raid it and the South. David and his men arrive on the third day to find it in ruins, and after the victory David returns there and sends plunder from it to Judah's towns.

l: Amalekites, The First Book of Samuel, Chapter 30
s: The Amalekites raid the South, Judah, Caleb's South, and Ziklag, burn Ziklag, and carry off the women and all who were in it without killing any. David's men find them spread over the ground eating, drinking, and dancing over the great plunder. David strikes them from twilight until the evening of the next day, and only four hundred young men on camels escape.

l: LORD, The First Book of Samuel, Chapter 30
s: The LORD answers David's inquiry through the ephod, telling him to pursue because he will surely overtake the raiders and recover all. David credits the LORD with preserving them and delivering the raiding troop into their hands, and calls the plunder taken from the LORD's enemies.

l: brook Besor, The First Book of Samuel, Chapter 30
s: The brook Besor is where David's six hundred men arrive and where those who are left behind stay. Two hundred men are too faint to cross it, so David continues with four hundred. David later meets the two hundred there on his return.

l: two hundred faint men (left at Besor), The First Book of Samuel, Chapter 30
s: Two hundred of David's men are so faint that they cannot cross the brook Besor and stay behind. On David's return they come out to meet him and the people with him, and David greets them. Despite objections, David rules that they receive the same share of the plunder as those who fought.

l: Egyptian servant, The First Book of Samuel, Chapter 30
s: A young Egyptian, servant to an Amalekite, is found in the field and given bread, water, a piece of fig cake, and two clusters of raisins, reviving him after three days and nights without food or drink. He explains that his master left him when he got sick three days earlier, and describes the raid including the burning of Ziklag. After David swears by God not to kill him or return him to his master, he leads David down to the Amalekite camp.

l: wicked men and worthless fellows, The First Book of Samuel, Chapter 30
s: Among those who went with David, these men say the two hundred who did not go will receive none of the plunder, only their wives and children to lead away. David rebukes them, calling them brothers, and rejects their proposal.

l: plunder (David's raid), The First Book of Samuel, Chapter 30
s: The Amalekites' plunder from the Philistines' land and Judah is recovered by David, with nothing lacking, small or great. David also takes the flocks and herds the Amalekites drove before their other livestock and calls them David's plunder. He shares it equally among all his men and sends part to the elders of Judah and many towns.

l: captives (families of David's men), The First Book of Samuel, Chapter 30
s: The wives, sons, and daughters of David's men, including David's wives Ahinoam the Jezreelitess and Abigail the wife of Nabal the Carmelite, are carried off alive by the Amalekites. David rescues them all, and none is lacking, whether small or great.

l: Amalekite raid on Ziklag, The First Book of Samuel, Chapter 30
s: The Amalekites raided the South, Judah, the Cherethites' South, Caleb's South, and Ziklag while David and his men were away, burning Ziklag and taking its people captive. The raid provokes the men's grief and anger toward David, and leads to his pursuit and the Amalekites' defeat.

l: statute of equal sharing, The First Book of Samuel, Chapter 30
s: David declares that the share of the one who goes down to battle and the one who stays with the baggage shall be the same: they shall share alike. He makes this a statute and an ordinance for Israel, which still stands at the time of writing.

l: The First Book of Samuel, The First Book of Samuel, Chapter 31
s: The Philistines fight Israel on Mount Gilboa, and the men of Israel flee and fall slain. The Philistines kill Saul's sons Jonathan, Abinadab, and Malchishua, and archers overtake Saul and badly wound him. Saul asks his armor bearer to kill him so the uncircumcised cannot abuse him; when the armor bearer refuses out of terror, Saul falls on his own sword, and the armor bearer then does likewise. Israelites across the valley and beyond the Jordan abandon their cities, and the Philistines occupy them. The Philistines cut off Saul's head, strip his armor, display it in the house of the Ashtaroth, and fasten his body to the wall of Beth Shan, but the valiant men of Jabesh Gilead retrieve the bodies at night, burn them, bury the bones under the tamarisk tree in Jabesh, and fast seven days.

l: Philistines, The First Book of Samuel, Chapter 31
s: The Philistines fought Israel, routed its men on Mount Gilboa, and killed Saul's three sons. They stripped the slain, cut off Saul's head, sent word throughout their land, placed his armor in the house of the Ashtaroth, and fastened his body to the wall of Beth Shan. They also moved into the cities Israelites abandoned.

l: Israel, The First Book of Samuel, Chapter 31
