s: The men of Israel fled before the Philistines and fell slain on Mount Gilboa. Those on the other side of the valley and beyond the Jordan, seeing the flight and the deaths of Saul and his sons, abandoned their cities, which the Philistines then occupied.

l: Saul, The First Book of Samuel, Chapter 31
s: Saul was overtaken by the Philistines and gravely distressed by their archers, and he lost his three sons in the battle. When his armor bearer refused to kill him, he fell on his own sword to avoid abuse by the uncircumcised. The Philistines later beheaded him, took his armor, and fastened his body to the wall of Beth Shan, until men of Jabesh Gilead took it down, burned it, and buried the bones.

l: Mount Gilboa, The First Book of Samuel, Chapter 31
s: Mount Gilboa was the site where the men of Israel fell slain before the Philistines. Saul and his three sons died there, and the Philistines found their bodies there the next day when they came to strip the slain.

l: sons of Saul, The First Book of Samuel, Chapter 31
s: Saul's sons Jonathan, Abinadab, and Malchishua were killed by the Philistines when they overtook Saul's company. The Philistines found their bodies on Mount Gilboa the next day, and their bodies were fastened to the wall of Beth Shan. The men of Jabesh Gilead later took them down, burned them, and buried their bones under the tamarisk tree in Jabesh.

l: armor bearer (Saul's armor bearer), The First Book of Samuel, Chapter 31
s: Saul's armor bearer refused to kill Saul because he was terrified. When he saw that Saul was dead after falling on his own sword, he likewise fell on his sword and died with him.

l: Beth Shan, The First Book of Samuel, Chapter 31
s: The Philistines fastened Saul's body to the wall of Beth Shan. The bodies of his sons were also on that wall until the valiant men of Jabesh Gilead took them down.

l: Jabesh Gilead, The First Book of Samuel, Chapter 31
s: Jabesh Gilead heard what the Philistines had done to Saul, and its valiant men acted in response. The bodies of Saul and his sons were brought there, burned, and their bones buried under the tamarisk tree in Jabesh.

l: inhabitants of Jabesh Gilead, The First Book of Samuel, Chapter 31
s: The inhabitants of Jabesh Gilead heard what the Philistines had done to Saul. All their valiant men went through the night, took the bodies of Saul and his sons from the wall of Beth Shan, and burned them in Jabesh. They buried the bones under the tamarisk tree and fasted seven days.

l: Battle of Mount Gilboa, The First Book of Samuel, Chapter 31
s: In this battle the Philistines fought Israel, whose men fled and fell slain on Mount Gilboa. Saul's three sons were killed, Saul was wounded by archers and died by his own sword, and his armor bearer and all his men died that same day. The defeat caused Israelites beyond the valley and the Jordan to abandon their cities to the Philistines.

l: Saul's death, The First Book of Samuel, Chapter 31
s: Saul, badly pressed by archers, asked his armor bearer to thrust him through so the uncircumcised could not abuse him. The armor bearer refused, so Saul fell on his own sword and died, and the armor bearer followed him in death. The Philistines then beheaded and stripped his body and fastened it to the wall of Beth Shan, and men of Jabesh Gilead later burned it and buried the bones.

l: The Second Book of Samuel, The Second Book of Samuel, The Second Book of Samuel / Chapter 1
s: After returning from slaughtering the Amalekites and staying two days in Ziklag, David receives a man from Saul's camp with torn clothes and earth on his head. The man, an Amalekite, reports that the people fled the battle and that Saul and Jonathan are dead, claiming he killed Saul at Saul's own request and brought David Saul's crown and bracelet. David and his men tear their clothes, mourn, weep, and fast for Saul, Jonathan, the people of the LORD, and the house of Israel. David then has the Amalekite struck down, saying his own mouth testified against him for slaying the LORD's anointed. David also laments Saul and Jonathan in a song, which he commands be taught to the children of Judah and which is written in the book of Jashar.

l: David, The Second Book of Samuel, The Second Book of Samuel / Chapter 1
s: David, back in Ziklag after slaughtering the Amalekites, questions the man who brings news of Saul's death and then tears his clothes and, with his men, mourns and fasts until evening. He has the Amalekite killed for stretching out his hand against the LORD's anointed, and composes a lamentation for Saul and Jonathan, calling Jonathan his brother whose love surpassed the love of women.

l: Saul, The Second Book of Samuel, The Second Book of Samuel / Chapter 1
s: Saul is reported dead after the battle on Mount Gilboa. According to the Amalekite's account, he was leaning on his spear with chariots and horsemen close behind, and asked the man to kill him because anguish had taken hold of him. David calls him the LORD's anointed and laments him as lovely and pleasant, swifter than eagles and stronger than lions, whose sword did not return empty.

l: Jonathan, The Second Book of Samuel, The Second Book of Samuel / Chapter 1
s: Jonathan is reported dead along with his father Saul, and David and his men mourn him. In David's lamentation his bow is said not to have turned back, he and Saul were not divided in death, and David calls him his brother whose love was wonderful to him.

l: Amalekite young man (the man who told David of Saul's death), The Second Book of Samuel, The Second Book of Samuel / Chapter 1
s: He comes to David from Saul's camp with torn clothes and earth on his head, reports the defeat and the deaths of Saul and Jonathan, and claims he killed Saul at Saul's request, bringing Saul's crown and bracelet to David. He identifies himself as the son of a foreigner, an Amalekite. David has him cut down, saying his blood is on his own head because his mouth testified that he had slain the LORD's anointed.

l: Israel, The Second Book of Samuel, The Second Book of Samuel / Chapter 1
s: Israel's people are reported to have fled the battle, with many fallen and dead. David and his men mourn for the people of the LORD and the house of Israel who fell by the sword, and the lamentation calls Israel's glory slain on its high places and tells the daughters of Israel to weep over Saul.

l: battle on Mount Gilboa, The Second Book of Samuel, The Second Book of Samuel / Chapter 1
s: The battle is known here through the Amalekite's report: the people fled, many fell, and Saul and Jonathan died, with Saul pursued by chariots and horsemen. In the lamentation David wishes that Gilboa's mountains have no dew or rain or fields of offerings, because the shield of the mighty was defiled and cast away there.

l: song of the bow (David's lamentation), The Second Book of Samuel, The Second Book of Samuel / Chapter 1
s: David sings this lamentation over Saul and Jonathan and commands that the children of Judah be taught it; it is written in the book of Jashar. It repeats the refrain "How the mighty have fallen," asks that the news not be told in Gath or Ashkelon, praises Saul and Jonathan, calls on Israel's daughters to weep for Saul, and mourns Jonathan as David's beloved brother.

l: The Second Book of Samuel, The Second Book of Samuel, Chapter 2
s: After inquiring of the LORD, David moves with his two wives and his men to Hebron, where the men of Judah anoint him king over the house of Judah, and he sends a message of blessing to the men of Jabesh Gilead for burying Saul. Meanwhile Abner, captain of Saul's army, takes Ishbosheth to Mahanaim and makes him king over Gilead, Ephraim, Benjamin, and all Israel. Abner's and Joab's forces meet at the pool of Gibeon, where twelve men from each side kill one another, and a severe battle follows in which Abner's men are beaten. Asahel pursues Abner despite warnings and is killed by Abner's spear, after which Abner appeals to Joab to stop the fighting and Joab blows the trumpet. David's side loses nineteen men and Asahel, while 360 of Benjamin and Abner's men die, and Joab's men bury Asahel in Bethlehem and reach Hebron by daybreak.

l: David, The Second Book of Samuel, Chapter 2
s: David inquired of the LORD and was told to go up to Hebron, where he settled with his two wives, Ahinoam and Abigail, and his men with their households. The men of Judah anointed him king over the house of Judah, and he reigned in Hebron seven years and six months. He sent messengers blessing the men of Jabesh Gilead for burying Saul and told them he would reward them.

l: Hebron, The Second Book of Samuel, Chapter 2
s: Hebron is the city the LORD directed David to go up to. David's men and their households lived in its cities, and the men of Judah anointed David king there. Joab and his men returned to Hebron at daybreak after burying Asahel.

l: Judah, The Second Book of Samuel, Chapter 2
s: The men of Judah came to Hebron and anointed David king over the house of Judah. The house of Judah followed David while Ishbosheth reigned over Israel.

l: Abner, The Second Book of Samuel, Chapter 2
s: Abner, son of Ner and captain of Saul's army, brought Ishbosheth to Mahanaim and made him king over Gilead, Ephraim, Benjamin, and all Israel. He proposed the contest at Gibeon, was beaten in the ensuing battle, and killed Asahel with the back end of his spear after warning him repeatedly to turn aside. He then appealed to Joab to end the pursuit and fled all night with his men to Mahanaim.

l: Ishbosheth, The Second Book of Samuel, Chapter 2
s: Ishbosheth, Saul's son, was taken by Abner to Mahanaim and made king over Gilead, the Ashurites, Jezreel, Ephraim, Benjamin, and all Israel. He was forty years old when he began to reign and reigned two years.

l: Joab, The Second Book of Samuel, Chapter 2
s: Joab, son of Zeruiah, led David's servants to meet Abner's party at the pool of Gibeon and accepted Abner's proposal for the young men to compete. He, with Abishai, pursued Abner after Asahel's death, then blew the trumpet to stop the fighting when Abner appealed to him. He gathered the people, found nineteen men and Asahel missing, and traveled all night to Hebron after burying Asahel.

l: Asahel, The Second Book of Samuel, Chapter 2
s: Asahel, one of the three sons of Zeruiah, was as light of foot as a wild gazelle and pursued Abner without turning aside. He refused Abner's warnings and was killed by the back end of Abner's spear. His body was buried in his father's tomb in Bethlehem.

l: contest at the pool of Gibeon, The Second Book of Samuel, Chapter 2
s: Abner proposed that young men compete before them at the pool of Gibeon, and twelve for Benjamin and Ishbosheth faced twelve of David's servants. Each seized his opponent and thrust a sword into his side, so all fell together, and the place was named Helkath Hazzurim. A very severe battle followed that day, in which Abner and the men of Israel were beaten by David's servants.

l: The Second Book of Samuel, The Second Book of Samuel, Chapter 3
s: The war between Saul's house and David's house continues, with David growing stronger and six sons being born to him in Hebron. After Ishbosheth rebukes Abner over Saul's concubine Rizpah, Abner angrily vows to transfer the kingdom to David and sends messengers offering an alliance. David demands the return of his wife Michal, whom Ishbosheth takes from her husband Paltiel, and Abner rallies Israel's elders and Benjamin before feasting with David in Hebron and leaving in peace. Joab, returning from a raid, accuses Abner of deceit and, without David's knowledge, has him brought back and kills him in the gate to avenge his brother Asahel. David publicly disowns the killing, curses Joab's house, mourns and fasts for Abner, and laments that the sons of Zeruiah are too hard for him.

l: David, The Second Book of Samuel, Chapter 3
s: David grows stronger, has six sons born to him in Hebron, and accepts Abner's alliance on the condition that Michal be returned to him. After Joab kills Abner, David declares himself and his kingdom guiltless, curses Joab's house, mourns and fasts, and admits he is weak and that the sons of Zeruiah are too hard for him.

l: Abner, The Second Book of Samuel, Chapter 3
s: Abner, strong in Saul's house, is rebuked by Ishbosheth over Rizpah, vows to transfer the kingdom to David, and persuades Israel's elders and Benjamin to turn to David. After feasting with David in Hebron and being sent away in peace, he is brought back from the well of Sirah and killed by Joab, and David mourns him as a prince and great man.

l: Joab, The Second Book of Samuel, Chapter 3
s: Joab returns from a raid with plunder, tells David that Abner came to deceive him, and secretly sends messengers to bring Abner back. He takes Abner aside in the gate and strikes him dead for the blood of his brother Asahel, and David curses his house.

l: Ishbosheth, The Second Book of Samuel, Chapter 3
s: Ishbosheth, Saul's son, asks Abner why he went in to Saul's concubine Rizpah, and is unable to answer Abner's furious reply because he fears him. He complies with David's demand and takes Michal from her husband Paltiel.

l: Saul’s house, The Second Book of Samuel, Chapter 3
s: Saul's house grows weaker and weaker during the long war with David's house. Abner, its strong man, vows to transfer the kingdom away from it to David.

l: David’s house, The Second Book of Samuel, Chapter 3
s: David's house grows stronger and stronger in the war against Saul's house. It gains an expectation that all Israel will come over to David through Abner's covenant effort, though Abner's death interrupts it.

l: Hebron, The Second Book of Samuel, Chapter 3
s: Hebron is where David's six sons are born, where Abner comes with twenty men and is feasted by David, and where Abner is brought back and killed in the gate. Abner is buried there, and David weeps at his grave.

l: Abner's murder, The Second Book of Samuel, Chapter 3
s: Joab takes Abner aside in the middle of the gate at Hebron and strikes him dead, avenging Asahel, with help from his brother Abishai. David did not know of it beforehand, declares himself guiltless, curses Joab's house, and leads public mourning, so that all Israel understands the king did not will it.

l: The Second Book of Samuel, The Second Book of Samuel, Chapter 4
s: After Abner dies in Hebron, Saul's son Ishbosheth and all Israel are discouraged. The text introduces Baanah and Rechab, Benjamite captains of raiding bands and sons of Rimmon the Beerothite, and notes Jonathan's lame son Mephibosheth. Rechab and Baanah enter Ishbosheth's house at midday, strike him on his bed, kill and behead him, and carry his head to David in Hebron, claiming the LORD has avenged the king on Saul. David rebukes them, recalling that he killed the man who brought news of Saul's death, and declares that wicked men who killed a righteous person in his bed must answer for his blood. David's young men kill the brothers, cut off their hands and feet, and hang them by the pool in Hebron, while Ishbosheth's head is buried in Abner's grave in Hebron.

l: Ishbosheth, The Second Book of Samuel, Chapter 4
s: Ishbosheth, Saul's son, grows feeble-handed when he hears Abner is dead in Hebron. He is struck, killed and beheaded on his bed at midday in his own house by Rechab and Baanah, and his head is later buried in Abner's grave in Hebron.

l: Baanah, The Second Book of Samuel, Chapter 4
s: Baanah, a Beerothite of Benjamin and son of Rimmon, is a captain of a raiding band serving Ishbosheth. With his brother Rechab he kills Ishbosheth, brings the head to David claiming the LORD's vengeance, and is then killed on David's order.

l: Rechab, The Second Book of Samuel, Chapter 4
s: Rechab, a Beerothite of Benjamin and son of Rimmon, is a captain of a raiding band serving Ishbosheth. With Baanah he murders Ishbosheth and presents the head to David, who has him killed, his hands and feet cut off, and his body hanged by the pool in Hebron.

l: David, The Second Book of Samuel, Chapter 4
s: In Hebron, David receives Ishbosheth's head from Rechab and Baanah and rejects their claim of vengeance, citing his earlier killing of the man who reported Saul's death in Ziklag. He orders the brothers killed and mutilated, and has Ishbosheth's head buried in Abner's grave.

l: murder of Ishbosheth, The Second Book of Samuel, Chapter 4
s: At the heat of midday, Rechab and Baanah enter Ishbosheth's house as if to fetch wheat, strike him in the body as he lies on his bed, kill and behead him, and escape by way of the Arabah through the night. They bring his head to David in Hebron, calling it the LORD's avenging of the king on Saul.

l: execution of Rechab and Baanah, The Second Book of Samuel, Chapter 4
s: David condemns Rechab and Baanah as wicked men who killed a righteous person in his bed and says he must require his blood from them. His young men kill them, cut off their hands and feet, and hang them beside the pool in Hebron.

l: The Second Book of Samuel, The Second Book of Samuel, Chapter 5
s: All the tribes of Israel come to David at Hebron, acknowledge him as their own flesh and bone, and anoint him king over Israel after making a covenant with him before the LORD. David, who began reigning at thirty and reigned forty years, takes the Jebusite stronghold of Zion and makes it David's city, growing greater because the LORD is with him. Hiram king of Tyre sends cedar, carpenters, and masons to build David a house, and David's sons born in Jerusalem are listed. When the Philistines go up to seek David, he inquires of the LORD twice: the first time he defeats them at Baal Perazim, and the second time he follows the LORD's instruction to circle behind them near the mulberry trees and strikes them from Geba to Gezer.

l: David, The Second Book of Samuel, Chapter 5
s: David is anointed king over all Israel at Hebron after making a covenant with the elders, having begun to reign at thirty and reigning forty years. He takes the stronghold of Zion, calls it David's city, builds there, and perceives that the LORD has established him. He also fathers more children in Jerusalem and defeats the Philistines twice by following the LORD's answers to his inquiries.

l: Israel, The Second Book of Samuel, Chapter 5
s: All the tribes of Israel come to David at Hebron, call themselves his bone and flesh, and recall that he led Israel out and in under Saul. Their elders make a covenant with him and anoint him king over Israel.

l: Hebron, The Second Book of Samuel, Chapter 5
s: Hebron is where the tribes and elders of Israel come to David, where he makes a covenant and is anointed king over Israel. David reigned there over Judah seven years and six months.

l: Jerusalem, The Second Book of Samuel, Chapter 5
s: Jerusalem is where David reigns thirty-three years over all Israel and Judah. David takes more concubines and wives from there, and the sons born to him there are named, including Solomon.

l: Jebusites, The Second Book of Samuel, Chapter 5
s: The Jebusites, inhabitants of the land, taunt David that the blind and the lame will keep him out of Jerusalem. David nonetheless takes their stronghold of Zion, and he calls for those lame and blind, hated by his soul, to be struck.

l: Zion, The Second Book of Samuel, Chapter 5
s: The stronghold of Zion is taken by David despite the Jebusites' boast that he could not enter. David lives in it and names it David's city.

l: LORD, The Second Book of Samuel, Chapter 5
s: The LORD, the God of Armies, is with David and makes him grow greater, and he established David as king over Israel for his people's sake. He answers David's inquiries, promising to deliver the Philistines in the first battle and giving a different plan for the second, signaling by the sound of marching in the mulberry trees that he has gone out before David.

l: Philistines, The Second Book of Samuel, Chapter 5
s: The Philistines go up to seek David after hearing he was anointed king, and spread themselves in the valley of Rephaim twice. David strikes them at Baal Perazim, where they leave their images behind, and later strikes them from Geba to Gezer.

l: David's covenant with the elders, The Second Book of Samuel, Chapter 5
s: King David makes a covenant with all the elders of Israel at Hebron before the LORD. After it, they anoint him king over Israel.

l: Battle at Baal Perazim, The Second Book of Samuel, Chapter 5
s: After the LORD tells David to go up and promises to deliver the Philistines, David strikes them at Baal Perazim. He says the LORD has broken his enemies like the breach of waters and names the place accordingly, and he and his men carry off the images the Philistines left.

l: The Second Book of Samuel, The Second Book of Samuel, Chapter 6
s: David gathers thirty thousand chosen men of Israel and sets out to bring God's ark from Baale Judah on a new cart driven by Uzzah and Ahio, sons of Abinadab. When Uzzah reaches out to steady the ark at the threshing floor of Nacon, the LORD strikes him dead, and David, displeased and afraid, leaves the ark in the house of Obed-Edom the Gittite. After the LORD blesses Obed-Edom's household for three months, David brings the ark into David's city with sacrifices, shouting, trumpets, and his own dancing in a linen ephod. Michal, Saul's daughter, despises him in her heart and rebukes him for uncovering himself, but David answers that he acted before the LORD who chose him over her father's house. The chapter ends noting that Michal had no child to the day of her death.

l: David, The Second Book of Samuel, Chapter 6
s: David gathers thirty thousand chosen men and sets out to bring up God's ark, but becomes displeased and afraid after Uzzah's death and diverts the ark to Obed-Edom's house. After hearing of the blessing on Obed-Edom, he brings the ark into his city with joy, sacrifices, dancing, and offerings, then blesses the people and gives them bread, dates, and raisins. He answers Michal's rebuke by saying he celebrated before the LORD, who chose him over Saul's house, and that he will be even more undignified.

l: ark of the covenant of God, The Second Book of Samuel, Chapter 6
s: The ark is carried on a new cart from Abinadab's house on the hill, and the cattle stumble at the threshing floor of Nacon. After Uzzah's death it stays three months in Obed-Edom the Gittite's house, then is brought into David's city and set in the tent David pitched for it. It is described as called by the Name, the name of the LORD of Armies who sits above the cherubim.

l: LORD, The Second Book of Samuel, Chapter 6
s: The LORD's anger burns against Uzzah, and he strikes Uzzah dead for his error beside the ark. He blesses Obed-Edom and all his house while the ark stays there. David says the LORD chose him above Saul and all his house to be prince over Israel.

l: Uzzah, The Second Book of Samuel, Chapter 6
s: Uzzah, a son of Abinadab, drives the new cart with his brother Ahio. When the cattle stumble, he reaches out and takes hold of the ark, and God strikes him dead there for his error.

l: Michal, The Second Book of Samuel, Chapter 6
s: Michal, daughter of Saul, watches from a window as the ark enters David's city and despises David in her heart for leaping and dancing. She confronts him, accusing him of shamelessly uncovering himself before his servants' maids. David rebuts her, and she has no child to the day of her death.

l: Obed-Edom, The Second Book of Samuel, Chapter 6
s: Obed-Edom the Gittite receives the ark into his house after David is afraid to move it on. The LORD blesses him, his house, and all that belongs to him during the three months the ark remains there.
